name: Linen-Waste
geological_features: White alkali flats stretching pole to pole
Remnant river deltas preserved in stone
specific_features: Bleached white surface resembling linen spread across the planet
Fossilized river delta systems from an ancient water cycle
description: Linen-Waste is a desert world bleached white by the alkali minerals that cover its surface like a linen shroud. The planet lost its water billions of years ago as its atmosphere thinned, and the evaporation of its ancient oceans and lakes left behind vast deposits of sodium carbonate, potassium salts, and borate minerals that now coat the surface in a brilliant white crust. From orbit, the planet gleams with the clean, flat whiteness of sun-bleached linen, broken only by the darker outlines of ancient geological features visible beneath the mineral deposits.

The thin atmosphere provides minimal protection from stellar radiation, and the white surface reflects enough light to create a glare that can damage unprotected eyes even through suit visors. The temperature swings are brutal, the alkali flats absorbing almost no heat during the day and radiating everything away at night. Dust storms occur but are unusual in their appearance—the white alkali dust creates whiteout conditions that are disorienting in a unique way, erasing all visual reference in a wall of blazing white rather than the darkness of typical dust storms.

The fossilized river deltas are Linen-Waste's most significant geological features, perfectly preserved beneath the mineral deposits. These deltas record the final millennia of the planet's water cycle in exquisite detail, with individual channel migrations traceable through the sediment layers. The water chemistry, reconstructed from the mineral deposits, tells the story of an ocean that grew progressively more alkaline as it shrank, concentrated by evaporation into a caustic brine before finally disappearing entirely. The last puddles must have been essentially liquid mineral concentrate, water in name only.

The mineral wealth of Linen-Waste is substantial and easily accessible, with boron compounds and lithium salts available in surface deposits that require no mining—merely collection and processing. Several automated harvesting operations extract these minerals for use in industrial and energy applications. The planet's bleakness discourages permanent habitation, but the economic value of its mineral deposits ensures a steady stream of robotic harvesters and periodic human inspection teams. Linen-Waste was once a world of rivers and oceans, and all that remains is the salt they left behind, a white memorial to water that will never return.
